final_recommendation: The room converged on a narrow labor-enforcement protocol amendment (14-day remediation clock, automatic suspension, joint inspection teams operational within 60 days) but failed to secure the final 8 votes needed for ratification. Congress explicitly stated labor's endorsement and Mexico's commitment get them to 210 votes, not 218. The credibility gap—whether Mexico will visibly enforce the mechanism before the floor vote—remains unresolved, leaving ratification prospects uncertain despite the amendment's technical adequacy.
minority_objections: Mexico refused to pre-commit to filing a specific enforcement action within 30 days post-ratification, citing sovereignty concerns and rejecting what it called 'pre-scripted performance for Congress.'
Labor and Congress demanded visible proof of enforcement (a filed case within 30 days) as the condition for unlocking the final 8 votes, which Mexico would not provide in writing.
key_conflicts: Mexico's sovereignty red line (will not pre-script enforcement actions on Congress's timeline) vs. Congress's credibility requirement (need visible enforcement proof before floor vote)
Labor's demand for binding 30-day enforcement commitment vs. Mexico's offer of 60-day operational readiness without case-filing guarantee
Canada's insistence on narrow amendment scope (labor only, no reopening) vs. implicit risk that failed ratification could trigger full renegotiation
key_concessions: Mexico accepted joint inspection teams with no veto power and 14-day automatic suspension mechanism, significant sovereignty concessions
Labor accepted 14-day remediation window (down from initial demands) and labor-commission enforcement path rather than direct trade penalties
Business accepted 60-day timeline for operational teams rather than immediate certainty
All parties agreed to narrow protocol amendment explicitly excluding dairy, Chapter 19, and other provisions to protect Canada's position
red_lines: Mexico: will not commit in writing to file specific enforcement action by day 30 post-ratification ('that turns sovereign enforcement into pre-scripted performance')
Congress: needs visible enforcement proof within 30 days or the final 8 votes don't materialize ('those votes don't come back until Mexico files a specific case')
Canada: amendment must remain labor-only; any reopening of full agreement puts dairy and Chapter 19 back in play, killing domestic ratification
Labor: automatic suspension with no political escape hatch; 'best efforts' language unacceptable
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: The 8-vote gap was treated as solvable through messaging/statements until R6, when it became clear it required proof of enforcement Mexico wouldn't provide
The room assumed Friday's coordinated statement would unlock ratification, underweighting that Congress's members might demand visible enforcement before voting
Canada's vulnerability if ratification fails (triggering full renegotiation) was acknowledged but not deeply explored as a forcing mechanism
The political sustainability of Mexico's commitment if labor groups demand manufactured complaints on Congress's timeline was raised by Mexico but not addressed by others
downstream_risk_variables: Whether Congress proceeds to floor vote with 210 votes (risking defeat) or delays until Mexico demonstrates enforcement
Whether failed ratification triggers full agreement reopening, exposing Canada's dairy concession
Whether Mexico's 60-day operational timeline proves credible or becomes a new point of contention
Whether labor unions publicly endorse the mechanism despite lack of 30-day enforcement guarantee, or withhold support
Whether media narrative shifts from 'deal has teeth' to 'deal stalled on enforcement proof' if Friday statement proceeds without Mexico's case-filing commitment
uncertainty_notes: The room achieved technical consensus on the enforcement mechanism (14-day clock, automatic suspension, joint teams in 60 days) but could not resolve the credibility gap: Congress needs 8 more votes that depend on visible proof of Mexico's enforcement, which Mexico will not pre-commit to providing on a fixed timeline. Whether ratification proceeds with 210 votes (risking floor defeat), delays until enforcement is demonstrated, or collapses entirely remains unresolved. Canada's position is protected only if the amendment doesn't trigger reopening, but failed ratification could do exactly that.

marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress explicitly stated 'votes aren't there as written' (R1), then '210 votes not 218' (R5-R6), with the final 8-vote gap unresolved and driving all of R5-R6's exchanges. This was the room's central problem.
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_pressure: Labor's demand for facility inspections, automatic suspension, and visible enforcement proof drove every round. R1: 'facility-level inspections with real teeth'; R2: 'automatic 30-day wage suspension'; R6: 'file first enforcement action within 30 days.' This shaped the entire amendment design.
marker_evidence.business_lobby_support: Business set 60-day deadline (R1), demanded written commitment by Friday (R2), and coordinated joint announcement (R3), but did not dominate the room's direction—labor enforcement and vote-counting did. Medium role.
marker_evidence.canadian_domestic_acceptability: Canada repeatedly insisted amendment stay narrow ('dairy and Chapter 19 back in play,' R1-R2) and demanded explicit protection language (R4). Important constraint but not the driving force—labor enforcement was.
marker_evidence.mexico_labor_sovereignty_risk: Mexico's refusal to pre-commit to enforcement action (R6: 'turns sovereign enforcement into pre-scripted performance') was a central, unresolved conflict that blocked the final 8 votes. This red line shaped the room's failure to converge.
marker_evidence.media_public_pressure: Media coordinated Friday narrative and Thursday briefing (R3-R4), but this was tactical support for the amendment, not a driving force. The room's direction was set by vote-counting and enforcement design, not media strategy.
marker_evidence.agreement_stability: Canada warned failed ratification could reopen the full agreement (R6: 'whole package gets reopened'), and the room treated amendment as necessary to avoid collapse, but this was a background constraint rather than the dominant thread. Medium role.
